why_this_tool: Kubeflow Pipelines shows every idea of the lesson in one place on a local cluster: containerized steps, typed inputs and outputs, tracked artifacts and a graph you can inspect.
alternatives: Flyte is also Kubernetes-native but enforces strongly typed tasks and versioned workflows with its own control plane; Prefect is a Python-first framework that runs flows on a laptop and scales out through work pools; Metaflow is a Python-first framework that moves local steps to remote compute with decorators; Argo Workflows is the general-purpose Kubernetes workflow engine with no ML artifact or lineage layer of its own.

setup.do: Read how Kubeflow is split into subprojects and confirm that Kubeflow Pipelines is the only one this path needs.
setup.done_when: You can name the Kubeflow subproject that runs pipelines and two subprojects you will not install.
setup.why: Kubeflow is a family of projects, not one binary. Knowing which piece does orchestration stops you from installing the whole platform on a laptop.

setup.do: Choose the standalone installation method for Kubeflow Pipelines and deploy it on a local Kubernetes cluster such as kind or minikube, with no cloud account and no GPU.
setup.done_when: All Kubeflow Pipelines pods in the local cluster report a running state.
setup.why: The installation methods differ a lot in footprint. The standalone subproject install is the one that fits in laptop memory.

setup.do: Install the Kubeflow Pipelines Python SDK into a fresh virtual environment.
setup.done_when: Importing the SDK in a Python session works and prints a version number.
setup.why: The SDK is the authoring interface: you write components and pipelines in Python and it compiles and submits them.

setup.do: Start a port forward to the Kubeflow Pipelines user interface and open it in a browser.
setup.done_when: The pipelines dashboard loads locally and shows an empty or sample list of runs.
setup.why: The user interface is where you read graphs, logs and artifacts for every run in the rest of this path.

steps.do: Run the getting started hello world pipeline against your local cluster from the SDK.
steps.done_when: The run appears in the user interface with a succeeded status and the greeting string as its output.
steps.why: One end to end run proves that the SDK, the API server and the cluster are talking to each other before you write anything of your own.

steps.do: Read why Kubeflow Pipelines exists and list what it adds on top of a plain task scheduler.
steps.done_when: You have a short written list of at least three things the pipeline platform gives you that a cron style scheduler does not.
steps.why: This is the lesson's first subtopic: ML-native orchestration means containerized steps, typed data passing and tracked artifacts, not just a schedule that happens to run ML code.

steps.do: Write two Python-based components, one that prepares a small dataset and one that trains a tiny CPU model on it.
steps.done_when: Both components compile without errors and each shows as a separate task when used in a pipeline.
steps.why: The component is the unit of the object model. Each one becomes its own container at run time, so writing two makes the isolation between steps visible.

steps.do: Write a pipeline that takes input parameters and wires the output of the first component into the second, then run it.
steps.done_when: The run graph in the user interface shows two connected nodes and the parameter values you supplied.
steps.why: A pipeline declaration is what turns separate components into a dependency graph. Data passing between tasks is what defines the execution order.

steps.do: Create a second version of the pipeline that adds control logic: a condition on a metric and a loop over two parameter values.
steps.done_when: The run graph shows the loop iterations as separate tasks and the conditional branch as taken or skipped.
steps.why: Real ML pipelines branch and fan out. Seeing how control logic changes the graph prepares you to read production pipelines.

steps.do: Configure a pipeline root for your pipeline so its artifacts land under a location you chose in the local object store.
steps.done_when: After a new run, the output artifacts are listed under the root path you configured rather than the default one.
steps.why: The pipeline root is where versioned artifacts persist. Controlling it is how a platform team separates projects and environments.

steps.do: Write an explicit input and output specification with a dataset artifact and a model artifact for your training component, then map each type to how Flyte would declare the same typed task.
steps.done_when: The run shows typed dataset and model artifacts on the task, and you have a short table mapping each one to its Flyte counterpart.
steps.why: Typed interfaces are the main idea Kubeflow Pipelines and Flyte share. Doing the mapping by hand shows where Flyte is stricter and where the two are equivalent.

steps.do: Run the Python function of one component directly on your laptop without the cluster, the way a Prefect flow or a Metaflow step starts locally.
steps.done_when: The function returns its result in a local Python session with no pod created, and you have noted what the local call skips compared with a cluster run.
steps.why: Prefect and Metaflow are Python-first and local by default. Trying the same loop in Kubeflow Pipelines shows how much, or how little, local iteration the Kubernetes-native tool gives you.

steps.do: Package one component as a containerized component with a pinned base image and pinned dependencies, built and loaded into the local cluster.
steps.done_when: The task pod for that component runs your own image tag and the run succeeds twice with identical outputs.
steps.why: A pinned image is what makes a step reproducible across laptops, CI and clusters. It is also the artifact a team actually promotes.

steps.do: Compare your standalone Kubeflow Pipelines install with the Kubeflow community distribution and decide which one a team in your situation should operate.
steps.done_when: You have a one paragraph decision naming who authors pipelines, where compute lives and which install you would promote to a shared cluster.
steps.why: Choosing an orchestrator is mostly about how much platform the team wants to run. The step from one subproject to the full distribution is that decision made concrete.

steps.do: Enable the MLflow integration against a local MLflow tracking server and rerun your pipeline so its parameters and metrics are recorded there.
steps.done_when: The local MLflow console shows a run for your pipeline with the same parameters and metrics as the Kubeflow Pipelines user interface.

verified.section_found: Visualize KFP Run Parameters and Metrics in MLflow

steps.why: Teams usually combine orchestrators and trackers rather than pick one. This integration shows Kubeflow Pipelines running the graph while MLflow holds the experiment record.

steps.do: Create a run of your compiled pipeline through the REST API from a small script, the way a CI job would trigger it.
steps.done_when: The script returns a run identifier and that run appears in the user interface without you clicking anything.
steps.why: Automation does not go through the user interface. Triggering runs over the API is how pipelines are wired into CI and into other orchestrators.
